topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks, six questions, sat every Summer. A displacement/time graph opened the paper in Summer 2024 (Q1: draw the graph 2, average speed 2) and the same picture returns inside the longer graph questions, as in Summer 2023 Q6. Expect two marks for a drawing, awarded one for two correct segments and one for the rest, then one or two marks per velocity read off it.
mustMemorise: Gradient of a displacement/time graph = velocity, with its sign
A horizontal section means the body is at rest, not that it is back at the start
Negative displacement means the other side of the starting point
The run of a stage is its own duration, not the clock reading at its end
Distance adds the sizes of the legs; displacement is the final reading on the vertical axis
notOnThisSpec: Curved displacement/time graphs and tangents drawn to them — Unit 2 keeps to straight sections with constant velocity
Calculus: a velocity is never found here by differentiating
Areas under a displacement/time graph, which carry no meaning
Motion that is not along one straight line

Read a velocity as the gradient of one section, using that section's own rise and run
Give a velocity with its sign, and a speed as the size of that velocity

sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2, g = 10 m/s². This topic sits at the front of the paper. Summer 2024 Q1 ran draw the graph (2 marks, one for any two correct segments and one for the rest) then calculate an average speed (2 marks). Later questions reuse the same reading inside longer graph questions. Parts here are marked in CCEA's MW and W: the method mark for the stage's change over its own time, the W mark for the value with its sign.
traps: Running the last section down to the time axis when the journey carries on past the starting point (Summer 2024 Q1)
Adding stages the journey never had, or taking the graph to a height it never reaches, such as a leg's length plotted as a position (Summer 2024 Q1)
Dividing by the clock reading at the end of a stage instead of the time that stage lasted (Summer 2023 Q6)
Handing in a velocity where the speed was asked, or the other way round (Summer 2019 Q2)
Dropping the minus sign from a velocity on a falling section
Reading a displacement off the axis when the question asked for a velocity
Using the total distance where the displacement was wanted, or the other way round
Calling a downward-sloping straight section a deceleration

noteBlocks.md: A distance/time graph only ever climbs, because distance keeps adding up. A displacement/time graph can come back down: its height is a live position, how far the body is from the chosen point, with a minus sign for the far side of it. Read a height and you have read where the body was at that moment.

noteBlocks.stem: Use the robot's graph to find its displacement from the pharmacy door when $t = 10$ s and when $t = 55$ s.

steps.decision: Go up from 10 to the first section and across to the axis. The section climbs 30 m in 20 s, so half way along it is at 15 m.
Up from 55 meets the falling section below the time axis: the robot is 6 m past the door, on the far side.

noteBlocks.prompt: The robot's graph is flat at 30 m from 20 s to 35 s. What is its displacement when $t = 30$ s, in metres?
noteBlocks.explain: The height of the graph is where the robot is. Straight up from 30 s meets the flat section, and across from there is 30 m, as in step 1 of See it: the robot is parked 30 m from the door.

twin.prompt: The robot's graph falls in a straight line from 30 m at $t = 35$ s to $-15$ m at $t = 60$ s. What is its displacement when $t = 45$ s, in metres?
twin.explain: It falls 45 m in 25 s, 1.8 m each second, so 10 s after the start of that section it is at $30 - 18 = 12$ m.

noteBlocks.caption: A stage's rise over its own run is its velocity.

noteBlocks.md: A straight section changes the displacement by the same amount every second, and that amount is the velocity. Take the two joints of the section: the rise is the finishing displacement minus the starting one, the run is the finishing time minus the section's own starting time. Rise over run, sign kept.

The size of the gradient is the speed and its sign is the direction: a steeper section means a faster body, whichever way it slopes, and a section sloping down means the body is moving back towards the start.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the velocity of the robot during the last section of its journey.

steps.decision: Write the two ends of the section as coordinates before anything else.
Finish minus start, both ways. The run is the time this section lasted, not the clock reading 60.
The minus sign is the direction: the robot is heading back towards the door.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Mechanics Further - Displacement Time
noteBlocks.why: A Northern Ireland teacher working from the CCEA Unit 2 specification: watch each section treated on its own before anything is added up.

noteBlocks.prompt: Work out the velocity of the robot during the first 20 seconds, in m/s.
noteBlocks.explain: The first section runs from $(0, 0)$ to $(20, 30)$: rise 30 m over its own run of 20 s, so $30 \div 20 = 1.5$ m/s, away from the door. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it on the first section.

twin.prompt: A straight section of a displacement/time graph runs from $(5, 12)$ to $(13, 44)$, with displacement in metres and time in seconds. What is the velocity, in m/s?
twin.explain: Rise $44 - 12 = 32$ m over a run of $13 - 5 = 8$ s: $32 \div 8 = 4$ m/s.

noteBlocks.md: Flat means the displacement is not changing, so the body has stopped: somewhere, not necessarily at the start. A falling straight section means the displacement is shrinking, so the body is heading back, at a steady negative velocity.

noteBlocks.title: Why falling is not slowing
noteBlocks.md: A straight section, however steep, has one gradient all the way along it, so the velocity does not change there. A line sloping down is a body going the other way at a steady rate, not a body slowing down.

steps.decision: Climbing straight: moving away from the start at a steady 4 m/s.
At rest for 8 s, 24 m from the start, not back at it.
Falling straight: a steady velocity back past the start, finishing 12 m beyond it. Nothing is slowing.

noteBlocks.prompt: The robot's last section falls in a straight line from 30 m to $-15$ m. What is the robot doing?
options: Travelling back past the pharmacy door at a steady velocity
Slowing down and stopping at the pharmacy door
Going downhill
noteBlocks.answer: Travelling back past the pharmacy door at a steady velocity
noteBlocks.explain: A straight falling section is one steady negative velocity: the body is coming back, and here it goes on below zero, past the door. This is step 3 of See it, where the trolley did the same.

twin.prompt: A straight section of a displacement/time graph falls from 10 m to $-5$ m. What is the body doing?
options: Moving back past its start at a steady velocity
Slowing down to a stop at its start
Moving down a slope
twin.answer: Moving back past its start at a steady velocity
twin.explain: Straight means steady; falling means heading back; ending below zero means past the start.

optionNotes.option: Slowing down to a stop at its start
optionNotes.why: Straight means steady: nothing is slowing, and it does not stop at the start, it passes it.
The height of the graph is a position along the line, not a height above the ground.

optionNotes.option: Slowing down and stopping at the pharmacy door
optionNotes.why: A falling line looks like something winding down, but a straight section has one steady velocity; it is heading back, not slowing.
The graph is not a picture of the corridor: its height is the distance from the door, not a height above the ground.

noteBlocks.md: Distance counts every metre covered, whichever way the body was going, so it only grows. Displacement is one signed reading at the end. For the distance take each sloping section, find the size of its change and add the sizes; for the displacement read one number off the axis.

steps.decision: The first sloping section climbs 25 m.
It falls from 25 m to $-35$ m: 25 m down to the axis and 35 m more. The size of the change is the distance for that leg.
Add the sizes; the flat section adds nothing.
One reading off the axis: 35 m on the far side of the door.

noteBlocks.prompt: A displacement/time graph rises from 0 m to 18 m, stays level, then falls in a straight line to −9 m. What total distance does the body travel, in metres?
noteBlocks.explain: Each leg counts as a length: 18 m out, then from 18 m down to $-9$ m, which is 27 m. So $18 + 27 = 45$ m. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it. The $-9$ is where it ends, its displacement, not a distance.

twin.prompt: A displacement/time graph rises from 0 m to 14 m, stays level, then falls in a straight line to −6 m. What total distance does the body travel, in metres?
twin.explain: 14 m out and 20 m back, from 14 m to $-6$ m: $14 + 20 = 34$ m.

noteBlocks.caption: Two bodies on one line: where their graphs cross, they are at the same place.

noteBlocks.md: Two bodies can share one set of axes, each line read exactly as before. Where the lines cross, the displacements are equal: the two bodies are at the same point, passing each other. Read the time off the bottom and the position off the side, and check it from the two velocities. Lines sloping opposite ways mean the bodies are moving towards each other.

noteBlocks.stem: P and Q move along the same straight track. When do they pass each other, and where?

steps.decision: Read straight down from the crossing to the time axis.

steps.working: P: velocity $300 \div 50 = 6$ m/s, so at $30$ s it is at $6 \times 30 = 180$ m
steps.decision: Check the reading from P's own gradient.

steps.working: Q: velocity $\dfrac{80 - 330}{50} = -5$ m/s, so at $30$ s it is at $330 - 5 \times 30 = 180$ m
steps.decision: Q starts 330 m out and comes back. The same 180 m: they pass there.

noteBlocks.prompt: On one displacement/time graph, A's line runs from (0, 0) to (40, 200) and B's from (0, 180) to (40, 20). At what time do they pass each other, in seconds?
noteBlocks.explain: A moves at $200 \div 40 = 5$ m/s and B at $\dfrac{20 - 180}{40} = -4$ m/s. They meet when $5t = 180 - 4t$, so $9t = 180$ and $t = 20$ s. This is steps 2 and 3 of See it: each position from its own velocity.

twin.prompt: On one displacement/time graph, A's line runs from (0, 0) to (30, 210) and B's from (0, 195) to (30, 15). At what time do they pass each other, in seconds?
twin.explain: A moves at 7 m/s and B at $-6$ m/s: $7t = 195 - 6t$, so $13t = 195$ and $t = 15$ s.

noteBlocks.md: **From words to a graph** (Summer 2024). The journey is told along a line through lettered points, and you draw it. Write each joint as a coordinate first; the last joint is wherever the words leave the body, not on the time axis.

**A rate from your own graph** (Summer 2024). The next part asks for an average speed or a velocity from what you drew. Take lengths from your joints; a velocity is one stage's own rise over its own run.
**Below the axis** (CCEA Teacher Guidance). A displacement can be negative: the body is past its start, on the far side. The graph carries on below the time axis; it does not stop at it.
**Two journeys, one grid** (Teacher Guidance; Summer 2023 and 2026 set two journeys on velocity/time graphs). Where two displacement lines cross, the bodies are at the same point.

noteBlocks.prompt: You have drawn a displacement/time graph but cannot see how to get the velocity of one stage. What is worth writing first?
options: The coordinates of the two ends of that stage
The total distance for the whole journey
The average speed
noteBlocks.answer: The coordinates of the two ends of that stage
noteBlocks.explain: A velocity is one stage's rise over its own run, and the two joints of that stage, written as coordinates, put both subtractions in front of you. That is what step 1 of See it does before anything else.

optionNotes.option: The total distance for the whole journey
optionNotes.why: It feels like progress, but a velocity belongs to one stage and needs that stage's own change and own time, not the whole trip.
An average covers the whole journey; the velocity of one stage is that stage's rise over its own run.

noteBlocks.prompt: A body goes 25 m out from O along a straight line, waits, then comes 40 m back along the line. Where does its displacement/time graph end?
options: At −15 m, below the time axis
On the time axis, at 0 m
At 40 m
At 15 m, above the time axis
noteBlocks.answer: At −15 m, below the time axis
noteBlocks.explain: Coming 40 m back from 25 m carries the body 15 m past O, to $25 - 40 = -15$ m, so the graph ends below the axis. This is step 3 of See it, where the trolley ended at $-15$ m too.

twin.prompt: A body goes 30 m out from O, waits, then comes 42 m back along the same line. Where does its graph end?
options: At −12 m, below the time axis
On the time axis, at 0 m
At 42 m
At 12 m, above the time axis
twin.answer: At −12 m, below the time axis
twin.explain: 42 m back from 30 m ends 12 m past O: $30 - 42 = -12$ m, below the axis.

optionNotes.option: On the time axis, at 0 m
optionNotes.why: Coming back further than it went takes the body past O, below the axis.
42 m is the return leg's length, not where the body ends.

optionNotes.option: At 12 m, above the time axis
optionNotes.why: It has gone past O, so the 12 m is on the far side: negative.

optionNotes.option: On the time axis, at 0 m
optionNotes.why: Stopping on the axis feels like getting home, but 40 m back from 25 m carries the body 15 m beyond O.
40 m is the length of the return leg, not a position; the graph ends at the displacement the body reaches.

optionNotes.option: At 15 m, above the time axis
optionNotes.why: The size is right, but the body has passed O, so it is on the far side: minus 15 m.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a straight line passes through $(2, 5)$ and $(6, 17)$. What is its gradient?
items.skill: Prerequisite: gradient of a straight line through two points

options.feedback: Rise $= 17 - 5 = 12$ and run $= 6 - 2 = 4$, so the gradient is $12 \div 4 = 3$.
That is the run on its own. The gradient divides the rise by the run.
That is the rise on its own. It still has to be divided by the 4 the line travels across.
The fraction is upside down: run over rise instead of rise over run.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a distance/time graph for a walk is a straight line from $(0, 0)$ to $(50, 400)$, with distance in metres and time in seconds. What is the walking speed?
items.skill: Prerequisite: speed from a distance/time graph

options.feedback: 400 m in 50 s, so $400 \div 50 = 8$ m/s. The gradient of a distance/time graph is a speed.
That divides the time by the distance. Speed is distance divided by time.
That is the distance covered. A speed needs the time underneath it.
Multiplying gives an area, which has no meaning on these axes. Divide instead.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a point R sits at $-37$ on a number line whose origin is O. How far is R from O?
items.skill: Prerequisite: size of a negative reading on a number line

options.feedback: The minus sign says which side of O the point is on. The distance is the size, 37.
A distance is a length, so it cannot be negative. The sign belongs to the position.
R is 37 away from O, not on top of it.
That is the distance from $-37$ to $+37$, twice as far as O.

items.stem: A displacement/time graph has a straight sloping section. What does the gradient of that section give?
items.skill: Name what the gradient of a displacement/time graph gives

options.feedback: Change in displacement divided by the time it took: that is a velocity, and it carries a sign.
Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity/time graph. A displacement/time graph is one step earlier than that.
Distance is read from the height of the graph, not from its slope. The slope tells you how quickly that height is changing.

options.text: The speed, so it is never negative
options.feedback: The gradient can be negative, and that minus sign is the direction. Speed is the size of the velocity, which is why it never carries one.

items.stem: Part of a displacement/time graph is a horizontal line for 15 seconds. What is happening?

options.text: The body is at rest for 15 seconds
options.feedback: The displacement is not changing, so the body is not moving. It is parked somewhere, not necessarily at the start.

options.text: The body is moving at a steady velocity for 15 seconds
options.feedback: A steady velocity would be a sloping straight line. Flat means the position stays the same.

options.text: The body is back at its starting point
options.feedback: That would be a section lying along the time axis. A horizontal line at any height means the body has stopped at that displacement.
Slowing down would show as a curve flattening. A straight horizontal line has already reached a velocity of zero and stays there.

items.stem: A section of a displacement/time graph slopes downwards. What does that tell you?

options.text: The body is travelling back towards, and possibly past, the starting point
options.feedback: A falling displacement means the position is decreasing, so the body has turned round.
Slowing down is about how the velocity changes, which a straight line cannot show. A constant negative gradient is a steady velocity in the other direction.

options.text: The body is below ground level
options.feedback: The vertical axis measures position along one straight line, not height. Negative simply means the other side of the starting point.

options.text: The body has a negative speed
options.feedback: Speed is a size and is never negative. The velocity is negative; its size is the speed.

items.stem: A body is at 60 m when $t = 20$ s and at 12 m when $t = 36$ s. What is its velocity over that stage?
items.skill: Use the stage's own time, not the clock reading

options.feedback: Rise is 12 - 60 = -48 m and run is 36 - 20 = 16 s, so the velocity is -48 divided by 16.
That divides by the clock reading of 36 s instead of the 16 s the stage actually took. Subtract the start time first.
The size is right, so the method mark is safe. The displacement is falling, so the velocity is negative.
That is the change in displacement, not the velocity. Divide it by the 16 s the stage took.

items.stem: A body goes 40 m forwards along a straight line and then 65 m backwards. What is its displacement from the start?

options.feedback: Displacement adds the signed legs: 40 - 65 = -25 m, which is 25 m on the other side of the start.
That is the total distance travelled. Displacement asks only where the body has ended up.
The size is right and the working is worth a method mark. The body finished behind the start, so the displacement is negative.
That would need the two legs to be equal. Here the return leg is 25 m longer than the outward one.

parts.stem:
A shuttle moves along a straight track. The graph shows its displacement from a marker, with displacement in metres and time in seconds.

Calculate the velocity of the shuttle during the first 10 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: (40 − (−20)) ÷ 10, the change from −20 m to 40 m over the stage's own time

hints: The graph starts at −20 m, not at zero.
The rise is 40 − (−20).
parts.workedSolution: Rise $= 40 - (-20) = 60$ m over a run of $10$ s, so the velocity is $\dfrac{60}{10} = 6$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides the height reached, 40 m, by the time. The shuttle started at −20 m, so it rose 60 m: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 m/s.

parts.stem:
Calculate the velocity of the shuttle during the last stage of its journey.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: −80 ÷ 20, the stage's change over its own time (accept 80 ÷ 20)

hints: The last stage runs from 25 s to 45 s.
It falls from 40 m to −40 m.
parts.workedSolution: Rise $= -40 - 40 = -80$ m over a run of $45 - 25 = 20$ s, so the velocity is $\dfrac{-80}{20} = -4$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right, so the method mark stands. The shuttle is heading back past the marker, so the velocity is −4 m/s.
The change of −80 m is right, but the method mark needs the 20 s this stage lasted; 45 is the clock reading at its end.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total distance travelled by the shuttle in the 45 seconds.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: both legs, 60 and 80, seen

hints: Take each sloping stage on its own.
From −20 m to 40 m is 60 m.
parts.workedSolution: First stage: from $-20$ m to $40$ m, $60$ m. Last stage: from $40$ m to $-40$ m, $80$ m. The level stretch adds nothing, so the total distance is $60 + 80 = 140$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the size of the change in displacement over the whole 45 s, from −20 m to −40 m. Distance adds the legs as lengths: 60 m and 80 m.
That reads each leg as the height it reaches, 40 and 40. The first leg starts at −20 m, so it is 60 m long, and the last falls 80 m.

context.setting: A coastguard launch on a straight channel

parts.stem:
A coastguard launch leaves a pier and moves along a straight channel.
It travels 100 m away from the pier at a constant velocity, taking 20 seconds.
It then stays where it is for 20 seconds.
Finally it turns and travels at a constant velocity in the opposite direction, passing the pier and stopping 20 m beyond it, taking 20 seconds.

On the grid, draw the displacement/time graph for the journey of the launch.

scheme.for: any two of the three line segments correct
the remaining line segment correct, finishing at (60, -20)

hints: Mark the joints first: (0, 0), (20, 100), (40, 100).
The last stage finishes below the time axis, at -20 m.
Join the joints with three straight lines and stop there.
parts.workedSolution: Three straight segments: from $(0, 0)$ up to $(20, 100)$; horizontal from $(20, 100)$ to $(40, 100)$; then down from $(40, 100)$ to $(60, -20)$, crossing the time axis at $t \approx 56.7$ s. Nothing is drawn after $t = 60$ s.

pattern.test: the last segment drawn down to the time axis: point plotted at (60, 0)

commonErrors.feedback: The launch does not stop at the pier: it carries on 20 m past it, so the last joint is $(60, -20)$, below the axis. Carrying the graph down to the axis is one of the slips the Summer 2024 examiners reported on this shape of question.

parts.stem:
Write down the length of time for which the launch is at rest.

Answer ________ s

scheme.for: 20 (seconds)

hints: Look for the horizontal section of your graph.
parts.workedSolution: The launch stays at 100 m from $t = 20$ s to $t = 40$ s, so it is at rest for $20$ s.

parts.stem:
Calculate the velocity of the launch during the first 20 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: 100 divided by 20

hints: Gradient of the first section.
Change in displacement divided by the time it took.
parts.workedSolution: Velocity $= \dfrac{100}{20} = 5$ m/s, away from the pier.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the run divided by the rise, which gives the seconds per metre. A velocity is metres per second, so divide the change in displacement by the time.

parts.stem:
Calculate the velocity of the launch during the last 20 seconds.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: the change in displacement over the stage's own time: −120 ÷ 20 (accept 120 ÷ 20)

hints: The launch goes from 100 m to -20 m.
Work out the change in displacement first, keeping its sign.
parts.workedSolution: Rise $= -20 - 100 = -120$ m over a run of $20$ s, so the velocity is $\dfrac{-120}{20} = -6$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right, so the method mark is yours. The launch is travelling back towards the pier, so the second mark needs −6 m/s.
The change of −120 m is right, but this part's method mark is for dividing by the 20 s the stage lasted (60 − 40); dividing by the clock reading of 60 earns nothing here.

parts.stem:
Eimear and Niall cycle along the same straight towpath. The graph shows their displacements from a bridge over the first 60 seconds.

Write down the velocity of Eimear.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: Her line runs from (0, 0) to (60, 480).
parts.workedSolution: Eimear's line rises $480$ m in $60$ s, so her velocity is $8$ m/s.

parts.stem:
Calculate the velocity of Niall.

Answer ________ m/s

scheme.for: the change in displacement over the time: −240 ÷ 60 (accept 240 ÷ 60)

hints: His line runs from (0, 300) to (60, 60).
He is getting closer to the bridge, so his velocity is negative.
parts.workedSolution: Niall's displacement changes by $60 - 300 = -240$ m in $60$ s, so his velocity is $\dfrac{-240}{60} = -4$ m/s.

commonErrors.feedback: That is Niall's speed. His displacement from the bridge is decreasing, so his velocity is negative; the method mark (M) is safe and the working mark (W) needs the sign.
That is where Niall starts, read off the displacement axis. A velocity is a gradient, so divide his change in displacement by the 60 s it took.

parts.stem:
Write down the displacement from the bridge at which the two cyclists pass each other.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: 200 (metres), read from the crossing point

hints: They pass where the two lines cross.
parts.workedSolution: The lines cross at $(25, 200)$, so they pass each other $200$ m from the bridge.

parts.stem:
Calculate how far apart the two cyclists are when $t = 60$ s.

Answer ________ m

scheme.for: 480 and 60 both read from the graph at t = 60

hints: Read both displacements at t = 60 s.
The gap between two bodies on the same line is the difference of their displacements.
parts.workedSolution: At $t = 60$ s, Eimear is at $480$ m and Niall is at $60$ m, so they are $480 - 60 = 420$ m apart.

commonErrors.feedback: Both readings, 480 m and 60 m, are right, and that is the method mark. They are on the same side of the bridge, so the gap between them is the difference: 480 − 60 = 420 m.

questions.solutionProgram: Eimear (0, 0) to (60, 480); Niall (0, 300) to (60, 60); meet when 8t = 300 - 4t; gap at t = 60 is 480 - 60

findTheMistake.stem: Siobhán is finding the velocity of a model train on the last stage of its journey. Its graph shows it 56 m from the station when $t = 14$ s and 16 m beyond the station when $t = 32$ s. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 takes the clock reading at the end of the stage. The stage began at $t = 14$ s, so it lasted $32 - 14 = 18$ s, and that is the run.
findTheMistake.feedback: The change in displacement is right, minus sign and all. The velocity needs it over the time the stage itself lasted. The Summer 2023 examiners saw times taken from the wrong starting point on a later journey; writing the two joints as coordinates first puts both subtractions in view.

findTheMistake.stem: Aidan is drawing the displacement/time graph of a trolley. It travels 30 m from O in 10 s, waits for 5 s, then travels 50 m back along the same line in 20 s. He works out the joints first:
studentWorking: Displacement at the end = 0 m, so the last joint is (35, 0)
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 ends the journey on the time axis, as if the trolley stopped at O. It comes 50 m back from 30 m, so it ends at $30 - 50 = -20$ m, 20 m past O, and the last joint is below the axis.
findTheMistake.feedback: Joints first is exactly the right habit, and the first two sections are right, which is the first mark. The Summer 2024 examiners saw weaker candidates carry the graph down to the time axis instead of to where the words leave the body.

prompts.answer: Its change in displacement divided by the time that stage took.
